| Dataset | Why it appears useful | What still needs checking |

| **[Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy (CHAS)](https://www.huduser.gov/PORTAL/datasets/cp.html)** — HUD; identifier **HUD044** | Custom Census tabulations describing housing problems and needs, particularly among low-income households. A good starting point for housing-needs assessments and local planning. | Available releases and geographies; exact cost-burden definitions, denominators, renter/owner breakdowns, uncertainty information, and access terms. The catalog labels its distribution “API,” but actual programmatic access has not been verified. |
| **[ACS 5YR CHAS Estimate Data by County](https://hudgis-hud.opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/HUD::acs-5yr-chas-estimate-data-by-county)** — HUD; ArcGIS item **dbcc9ba4a4144a6d823b4d429d2b97c6** | The most immediately promising option for county mapping and comparisons. Metadata describes household counts by housing problems and income categories, including 30%, 50%, and 80% of HUD’s area median family income. CSV, Excel, and GIS distributions are listed. | **Coverage is 2016–2020**, explicitly stated in the description—not current conditions. Check for newer releases, field definitions, geographic identifiers, missing/suppressed values, and appropriate denominators before calculating shares. This is a CHAS delivery product, not an independent corroborating source. |
| **[Housing Affordability Data System (HADS)](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/hads/hads.html)** — HUD; identifier **HUD031** | AHS-derived files classify housing units and households using affordability, income, Fair Market Rent, poverty income, and owner/renter housing-cost burden. Promising for historical affordability research. | Metadata says **2013 is the latest public-use file**, with 2015 onward available only as internal-use files. Confirm present availability and access restrictions, geographic detail, survey documentation, and comparability across years. |
| **[Seattle Mandatory Housing Affordability Zones](https://data-seattlecitygis.opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/SeattleCityGIS::mandatory-housing-affordability-mha-zones)** — Seattle; ArcGIS item **cce94a62698640b59031ae35292acfe5** | Useful for mapping where affordable-housing development requirements **may apply**. Provides local policy context rather than household affordability outcomes. | The publisher explicitly says it is **not an official zoning map**. Verify current legal requirements, effective dates, parcel applicability, and authoritative zoning before use. |

### Recommendation
Start with **CHAS**, then choose the geography and observation period needed. Use **HADS** for historical household analysis and Seattle’s layer only for that city’s policy geography.

No. A **catalog harvest date** records when a catalog collected or refreshed a dataset’s metadata—not when the underlying observations were measured.

To identify an observation year, inspect:
- The dataset’s **temporal coverage**.
- Dates or year fields in the actual data.
- Source documentation defining the reference period.

Also distinguish an observation period from a **release date** or **revision date**. For example, data harvested in 2024 could contain 2022 observations, a series spanning many years, or revised historical values.

If the observation period is not documented, report it as **unknown** rather than infer it from the harvest date.

**Not with a simple average.** County unemployment rates use the **civilian labor force**, not total population, as their denominator. An unweighted average would give a small county the same influence as a large one.

The appropriate aggregation is:

\[
\text{State unemployment rate}
=100\times\frac{\sum \text{county unemployed}}{\sum \text{county civilian labor force}}
\]

This is equivalent to a **labor-force-weighted average** of county rates when using unrounded rates and consistent underlying data. Do not weight by total population.

Use the same observation period and measure throughout—for example, annual-average, not-seasonally-adjusted figures—and include all constituent jurisdictions (including Baltimore city for Maryland). For the official state figure, use the published state rate rather than reconstructing it from rounded county rates.

Source: BLS *Local Area Unemployment Statistics*, identifier **DOL-BLS-3060-01**; the registered aggregation rule is “do not average county rates; use summed unemployed and labor force.” [Maryland source data](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/la/la.data.27.Maryland).
